title: Photo 51 had two names behind it.
description:
Photo 51 had two names behind it. KCL and UKRI say it was taken by Rosalind Franklin with her PhD student Raymond Gosling at King's College London in May 1952.

King's College London says the DNA was exposed to X rays for a total of 62 hours to take Photograph 51.

Watson saw it in January 1953. KCL says Wilkins showed it to him, having a copy because he was soon to take over the work. KCL says Franklin was unaware.

Wilkins had it legitimately, says UKRI. UKRI says it was part of her papers as she was leaving for Birkbeck, and notes some people think he should not have shared it without her knowledge or permission.

KCL says Photograph 51 was published in a paper by Franklin and Gosling, in the same issue as Watson and Crick's paper.

The 1962 Nobel Prize went to three men. Wilkins, Watson and Crick shared it. Franklin died in 1958, and History notes the Nobel Foundation does not award prizes posthumously.

The evidence was public in 1953. The prize came nine years later.

Sources:
- https://www.kcl.ac.uk/the-story-behind-photograph-51: read (King's College London, Brian Sutton, 14 April 2023). Established that Photograph 51 was taken by Rosalind Franklin together with PhD student Raymond Gosling at King's in May 1952, that the DNA was exposed to X rays for a total of 62 hours, that Wilkins showed it to Watson in January 1953 because he had a copy and was soon to take over the work, that Franklin was unaware it had been shown, and that it was published in Nature on 25 April 1953 in a paper by Franklin and Gosling alongside Watson and Crick's.
- https://ukri.org/blog/from-the-archive-rosalind-franklins-famous-photo-51: read (UKRI). Established the May 1952 date and the Franklin and Gosling credit, that some people think Wilkins should not have shared it without her knowledge or permission, and the defence that he had it legitimately as part of her papers because she was soon to leave for Birkbeck College.
- https://www.history.com/articles/rosalind-franklin-photo-51-dna: read (History, Becky Little, 28 May 2025). Established the 62 hours, the three papers in the April 1953 issue of Nature, Franklin's death in 1958, and that Wilkins, Watson and Crick shared the 1962 Nobel Prize, which is not awarded posthumously.
